examples.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s) = \mathcal L\{f(t)\},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14043349/assets/e70e54b6a70cebd480b86baf9d0e1d90bde0b3d9277c982d5d5e77218d0d2f5d.png)
examples.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14043349/assets/48965cee8a09df4f637b4d997fdb9c90673e69a90ea1320434f9b471a2fed280.png)

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{2t-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{(2-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s \leq 0.$

For $s > 0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{(2-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2-s}{[{e}^{(2-s)t}]}_{0}^{3}+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{-{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{3}^{a} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-as}-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot (0-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}+\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s > 0.$

feedback.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)=u(t-3)$ and $u$ is the unit step function.

$F(s)=L{f(t)}=$
{{field-1}},
valid for $s\,$
{{field-2}}{{field-3}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-3)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<3 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }u(t-3){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{3}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-sa}-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{s}(0-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
L{f(t)}=\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s},\,s>0.
$$
